paragraphs.text: Tribute: taxes that an occupied people pay to the one who enslaves them.

The prophet marvels at the destruction that has come upon Jerusalem and likens her to a great lady who has become a sorrowful widow, rejected by others. After Jerusalem was a great city full of inhabitants, she has now become a ruin, and the weak Jews who remain in her are enslaved to Babylon and pay tribute.

When a person forsakes God, Satan humiliates him, so he withdraws from all the believers, feels lonely, and devotes his strength to evil. Consider the consequences of sin so that you may keep away from it, and do not let its pleasures allure you, for they are deceptive and temporary, hiding behind them humiliation and torment.

He portrays the isolation of Jerusalem as a widow weeping alone in the night, when all who were allied with her are asleep. All have abandoned her, and she sits in sorrow, weeping over the destruction that has come upon her. This is a symbol of the human soul that sits in the darkness of sin, suffering its consequences and grieving over all that has befallen it after all those who encouraged it to do evil have abandoned it.
He explains the state of Jerusalem, taken captive by Babylon, as follows:
1- She became enslaved to Babylon and humiliated.
2- The loss of peace and rest, while the nations around her rejoice and enjoy themselves.
3- She could not flee and be saved from the Babylonian siege; rather, the armies of Babylon were able to enter the city, destroy it and burn it, so the people were in great distress.
Zion: what is meant is Jerusalem, for it is her ancient name.
He continues explaining the state of humiliated Jerusalem as follows:
1- Jerusalem was deprived of keeping the feasts of the Lord, because she had been destroyed and the Jews no longer came from all the lands to Jerusalem to keep the feast.
2- The gates of Jerusalem were broken and burned, that is, she lost her security and protection.
3- The priests who lead the worship in the temple of Jerusalem were in deep sorrow, because the temple had been burned and they could not offer the sacrifices and serve God.
4- The sorrow of her virgins, meaning the bitterness of all the souls in her, since they weep over the ruin of their great city.
[2] Sin is the cause of humiliation (vv. 5-9)

5- Her adversaries are the chief, her enemies prosper; for the LORD hath afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions: her children are gone into captivity before the enemy. 6- And from the daughter of Zion all her beauty is departed: her princes are become like harts that find no pasture, and they are gone without strength before the pursuer. 7- Jerusalem remembered in the days of her affliction and of her miseries all her pleasant things that she had in the days of old, when her people fell into the hand of the enemy, and none did help her: the adversaries saw her, and did laugh at her destruction. 8- Jerusalem hath grievously sinned; therefore she is become an abomination: all that honoured her despise her, because they have seen her nakedness: yea, she sigheth, and turneth backward. 9- Her filthiness is in her skirts; she remembereth not her last end; therefore she came down wonderfully: she had no comforter. O LORD, behold my affliction: for the enemy hath magnified himself.

The enemies of Jerusalem grew great and ruled over her like chiefs, while she was in humiliation, because the Lord Himself permitted this as discipline for her sins, whether because of the worship of idols or evil lusts. The enemy seized the best of her sons and took them to Babylon as slaves.

Sin makes a person lose his strength. So remember, my brother, that you are the image of God and a temple of His Holy Spirit, so live for Him and do not defile yourself with sin; thus you keep your strength and rejoice with God.
Harts: a kind of deer that moves swiftly.

Because of the evils of Jerusalem, she lost all her greatness and beauty and her chiefs who led her and managed her affairs, for they were in great fear before the enemy and fled swiftly, as harts run far away in search of food when they find no pasture to eat in. For Jerusalem was in hunger and those in her were about to die, so the king and the chiefs made a breach in the wall of the city and fled from it. But the enemy's armies seized them and killed them, and humiliated the rest of them, who became extremely weak, and Babylon took them captive. The armies of Babylon pursued everyone who tried to flee and seized him.

During the destruction of Jerusalem she remembered her worldly lusts and the evils in which she had been immersed, and saw that she had lost all her pleasures. He portrays Jerusalem as a woman staggering from weakness and fear before the enemy, and in her humiliation the Babylonian enemies mocked her, corrupted her and destroyed her.
Abomination: filthy and despised.
Her nakedness: he likens Jerusalem to a woman who came into shame after being stripped of her garments, that is, she became a ruin with no glory in her.

He makes clear that the humiliation and contempt that came upon Jerusalem are because of her sin. All the neighbors of Jerusalem who used to honor her despised her while she was in shame, for there was no longer in her the temple or palaces, but the stinking corpses of the slain, and the rest of her sons had fled from her or been taken by the enemy into captivity.

He likens Jerusalem to an adulterous woman whose skirts reveal her uncleanness and her fall into evil, that is, the cause of Jerusalem's destruction is her fall into unclean lusts. Sadly, when Jerusalem was immersed in uncleanness she forgot that she was a daughter of God and did not prepare for her eternal life. Therefore, when the wrath of God came upon her, she found no one to comfort her in her sorrow, because it is God who comforts and supports His children; if they forsake Him they will find no one to comfort them and make them glad, but will be in deep sorrow.
But the prophet returns to God on behalf of Jerusalem and asks for His mercies, and that He remove from him the Babylonian enemy who has become proud and humiliated the people of God.
[3] The defilement of the temple (vv. 10, 11)

10- The adversary hath spread out his hand upon all her pleasant things: for she hath seen that the heathen entered into her sanctuary, whom thou didst command that they should not enter into thy congregation. 11- All her people sigh, they seek bread; they have given their pleasant things for meat to relieve the soul: see, O LORD, and consider; for I am become vile.
Her sanctuary: the temple of the Lord.

The sorrow of Jerusalem was great because of the enemy's control over the whole city, but the most important thing in her is the temple of the Lord, which no pagan person may enter. Now, however, the Babylonians entered it, defiled it and burned it, after stealing the precious possessions in it.

When Babylon besieged Jerusalem, the food inside ran out and hunger grew severe among the people, and they tried to buy bread by offering the dearest things they had, that they might live. Then Jerusalem sighs in sorrow and asks for God's help because of the humiliation into which she has fallen.

The devil tries to deprive you of the bread of life, that is, Christ our God, and besieges you with sin so that you may go away from God. So do not yield to him, but hold fast to your God and remain in His Church, nourished by her Holy Sacraments and His satisfying word.
[4] The Lord disciplines His people (vv. 12-16)

12- Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow, which is done unto me, wherewith the LORD hath afflicted me in the day of his fierce anger. 13- From above hath he sent fire into my bones, and it prevaileth against them: he hath spread a net for my feet, he hath turned me back: he hath made me desolate and faint all the day. 14- The yoke of my transgressions is bound by his hand: they are wreathed, and come up upon my neck: he hath made my strength to fall, the Lord hath delivered me into their hands, from whom I am not able to rise up. 15- The Lord hath trodden under foot all my mighty men in the midst of me: he hath called an assembly against me to crush my young men: the Lord hath trodden the virgin, the daughter of Judah, as in a winepress. 16- For these things I weep; mine eye, mine eye runneth down with water, because the comforter that should relieve my soul is far from me: my children are desolate, because the enemy prevailed.

He likens Jerusalem to a woman looking at those who pass by on the roads leading to her, while she is in ruins and sorrowful over her destruction. She calls to the passers-by to see how great her sorrow is, because God permitted her humiliation on the day of Babylon's attack upon her.

Jerusalem continues speaking to the passers-by and tells them that God sent fire and it burned her bones. She is like a woman who has been shattered, since the Babylonians burned the temple of God and the palaces of Jerusalem. Her fall into the hand of Babylon is likened to Babylon spreading a net into which Jerusalem fell as prey, and Babylon seized her; whoever could flee from Jerusalem fled, and whoever remained in her was left in perpetual humiliation and sorrow.
Yoke: a piece of wood placed on the necks of two animals to pull agricultural implements, and it is tied to the animal's neck by a wreathed rope, that is, a strong one.

Jerusalem also likens herself to an animal on whose neck the yoke has been placed, then God brought a wreathed rope and tied her neck to the yoke with it. He means that she has become enslaved to Babylon in weakness and humiliation and has lost her strength, since she fell into strong hands, the hands of Babylon.

Jerusalem declares that it is God who permits these disciplines. It is He who permitted all her strong sons, who were able to fight, to be despised, so they became weak, and her young men, that is, her strength, were crushed, because youth is distinguished by strength. Jerusalem likens herself to a virgin who has been put in a winepress, so her blood flowed and all her strength was lost.

The comforter that should relieve my soul: what is meant is God, who is able to comfort me and restore my soul to me so that I may live. What increased Jerusalem's sorrow most is her knowing that the discipline is from God, who used to comfort her and give her life in the midst of tribulations, whereas now it is He who permitted the tribulations to discipline her, and He will not comfort her because of her evil. And whenever Jerusalem looked at her slain children, their corpses lying in the streets, and at the cruelty of the Babylonian enemy, her tears flowed.

Accept God's discipline and hasten to repentance, for He is merciful and ready to remove His wrath if you return to Him. Do not despair if the tribulations increase, for He is able to remove them from you however hard the circumstances may be.
[5] Jerusalem without a comforter (vv. 17-19)

17- Zion spreadeth forth her hands, and there is none to comfort her: the LORD hath commanded concerning Jacob, that his adversaries should be round about him: Jerusalem is become unclean among them. 18- The LORD is righteous; for I have rebelled against his commandment: hear, I pray you, all people, and behold my sorrow: my virgins and my young men are gone into captivity. 19- I called for my lovers, but they deceived me: my priests and mine elders gave up the ghost in the city, while they sought their meat to relieve their souls.

The prophet Jeremiah likens Jerusalem to a weak woman stretching out her hands, asking for help in the face of the Babylonian attack, but sadly she found no one to help her, because God commanded that she be disciplined, so all her allies, whether Egypt or all the lands around her, abandoned her. Thus the Babylonian siege remained around Jerusalem, then the Babylonian army entered, defiled the temple and ruined all Jerusalem.

Jerusalem confesses her sins and her disobedience to God, who caused this ruin, and Jerusalem looks in sorrow as she sees her young men and youths taken as slaves into captivity with no one to help her. She calls to the nations around her, but no one moves to support her and rescue her from the hand of Babylon.

Jerusalem declares with regret that all her allies who loved her and promised to help her have abandoned her, and more than this, that the priests and the elders sought to save themselves and left the people to perish at the hand of Babylon. The priests and the chiefs tried to flee from Jerusalem, but the enemy seized them.
Do not trust in the arm of flesh, for men are not reliable and their promises are false; but trust in God, for He will save you however great the danger, and His promises are true forever.
[6] A cry to God (vv. 20-22)

20- Behold, O LORD; for I am in distress: my bowels are troubled; mine heart is turned within me; for I have grievously rebelled: abroad the sword bereaveth, at home there is as death. 21- They have heard that I sigh: there is none to comfort me: all mine enemies have heard of my trouble; they are glad that thou hast done it: thou wilt bring the day that thou hast called, and they shall be like unto me. 22- Let all their wickedness come before thee; and do unto them, as thou hast done unto me for all my transgressions: for my sighs are many, and my heart is faint.
As death: those who remain in the house are in terror and fear, like the dead.
Bereaveth: it kills the young men, so their mothers are left without children, that is, bereaved.

Jerusalem cries out, and her heart boils with emotion over her slain and the humiliation into which she has come. She likens herself to a woman whose heart is violently moved and troubled within her for her young men, whose corpses lie in the streets, so Jerusalem became like a bereaved mother, and those who remained in the houses of Jerusalem became like the dead from fear.

Jerusalem says that when the nations around her heard of her trouble, no one helped her; rather, they gloated over her and rejoiced at her ruin. But she trusts that God will punish these wicked ones who gloat over her.

Jerusalem cries out to God to take vengeance on her neighbors who gloat over her, and, as He disciplined her with destruction, to punish them also. Jerusalem says this out of the abundance of her sorrow, which has left her unaware.
Cry out to God in all your tribulations and trust that He loves you; He disciplines you for a time so that you may return to Him and obtain His mercies.
The wrath of God upon Jerusalem

When Babylon attacked Jerusalem and destroyed everything in her, it deprived her of life. This is likened to the darkness that settled upon her, because of the darkness of her sin, since darkness is a symbol of sin and its evil effects. The prophet marvels in sorrow at Jerusalem's loss of all her glory and pride, which was the temple of God. Jerusalem was called the city of God among the peoples, and he calls it the footstool of God, that is, His place on earth, because in the eyes of men He dwells in heaven, as He is exalted above their thoughts; but His dwelling on earth is in His temple in Jerusalem, which was fulfilled by His Incarnation and His dwelling in His Church in the New Testament. Jerusalem was exalted by her faith and her worship of God, but she was cast down from heaven to earth when she worshiped idols and walked in her evil lusts, so she lost her pride and Babylon destroyed her.

Long ago God promised Jacob, the father of the fathers who dwelt in tents, blessing and good, but his offspring, that is, Jerusalem and Judea, walked in evil, so God swallowed up their dwellings, which are their tents, by the hand of Babylon; that is, God destroyed their dwellings so that they no longer existed, as a beast swallows its prey so that it no longer exists. He speaks of their dwellings as tents to remind them that they are strangers in the world, and that their hearts should be set on heaven and not on earthly lusts. Therefore, when they immersed themselves in lusts they lost their place and their city was destroyed.

Jerusalem relied on her walls and fortresses to protect her and did not trust in God, and she lived in her sins; therefore He destroyed her material strength, that is, her strongholds. By saying Judah he means the whole kingdom of Judah, that is, Jerusalem and Judea. The destruction was violent, so the palaces were leveled to the ground, and God permitted the Babylonians to defile the temple by entering it, and by entering the palaces of the chiefs and destroying everything.
Cut off: broken.

The horn represents strength in an animal, with which it attacks other animals. Here the strength of Israel is likened to strong horns, but God broke them when He was angry with her by means of Babylon.
The right hand represents strength. God abandoned His people by drawing back His right hand, and He left Babylon to crush His people as discipline for them, that they might repent.
He also likens God's power that disciplines His people to the fire that burns His people, and this is what happened when Babylon burned the temple of God and the palaces of Jerusalem.
Tabernacle: the inner part of the tent, which is not visible to those around it.

God likens Himself to a warrior who holds the bow and shoots arrows at His people as discipline for them. Thus God appeared as an enemy to His people while disciplining them by the hand of Babylon, but He is the loving Father who wants their repentance and their return to Him. God set His right hand, that is, His power, against His people, as though He hated them, and this through the armies of Babylon, whereas in truth He wants, by His discipline, their return to Him.
And everything Jerusalem possessed and kept in her palaces of what is pleasant to man, God destroyed and slew, whether people or their possessions and treasures that they had hidden in their houses.
God's wrath appeared like that of one enraged at another, and like a mighty one pouring out fire, so Jerusalem burned. All this was accomplished by the hand of Babylon.
By God's rising up as an enemy against His people and destroying the palaces and fortresses of His city Jerusalem, her sorrow became great.

Know that your sin is a defiance of God that deserves death, and God is long-suffering toward you so that you may repent. So do not persist in evil, lest the wrath of God come upon you, but hasten to repentance to obtain His mercies, and know that He, as a Father, seeks your salvation, even through tribulations.
[2] The rejection of her worship (vv. 6, 7)

6- And he hath violently taken away his tabernacle, as if it were of a garden: he hath destroyed his places of the assembly: the LORD hath caused the solemn feasts and sabbaths to be forgotten in Zion, and hath despised in the indignation of his anger the king and the priest. 7- The Lord hath cast off his altar, he hath abhorred his sanctuary, he hath given up into the hand of the enemy the walls of her palaces; they have made a noise in the house of the LORD, as in the day of a solemn feast.

Here he speaks of God's rejection of His people's worship of Him, by removing His tent of meeting with them, which became the temple of Solomon, which was in great Jerusalem, which he calls a garden because of her glory. God destroyed the Jews who used to gather for worship in His temple, and thus God despised the feasts of the Jews, which they call solemn feasts, among them the Sabbath day, because His people had become sin; and God did not honor even the chiefs, such as the king and the priest, because they were corrupt and led the people astray.

By burning the temple and destroying Jerusalem, God declared His rejection of the sacrifices of the Jews and of everything they consecrate to Him. More than this, He permitted the enemies to tear down the walls and humiliate the people, and so the cries of the Jews rose as in the feasts and solemn feasts, but here they were cries of sorrow instead of the voices of joy in the feasts.
Do not persist in some sin and neglect it, lest God reject your prayers and your worship. It is better for you to repent, so that your prayers become deeper and more acceptable to God.
[3] Her humiliation (vv. 8-14)

8- The LORD hath purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion: he hath stretched out a line, he hath not withdrawn his hand from destroying: therefore he made the rampart and the wall to lament; they languished together. 9- Her gates are sunk into the ground; he hath destroyed and broken her bars: her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: the law is no more; her prophets also find no vision from the LORD. 10- The elders of the daughter of Zion sit upon the ground, and keep silence: they have cast up dust upon their heads; they have girded themselves with sackcloth: the virgins of Jerusalem hang down their heads to the ground. 11- Mine eyes do fail with tears, my bowels are troubled, my liver is poured upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people; because the children and the sucklings swoon in the streets of the city. 12- They say to their mothers, Where is corn and wine? when they swooned as the wounded in the streets of the city, when their soul was poured out into their mothers' bosom.

13- What thing shall I take to witness for thee? what thing shall I liken to thee, O daughter of Jerusalem? what shall I equal to thee, that I may comfort thee, O virgin daughter of Zion? for thy breach is great like the sea: who can heal thee? 14- Thy prophets have seen vain and foolish things for thee: and they have not discovered thine iniquity, to turn away thy captivity; but have seen for thee false burdens and causes of banishment.
Line: a string that the builder uses to make sure the wall is straight and does not lean.
Rampart: walls built to defend the city.

In God's wrath against Jerusalem He wanted to remove protection from her by tearing down her walls. Here the line is used figuratively, for the line is used to keep the building true, and God sets right Jerusalem, crooked with her sins, by tearing her down so that she may be disciplined and repent. God continued destroying Jerusalem by the hand of Babylon, for His stretched-out hand, which is Babylon, does not hesitate until Jerusalem is ruined; therefore the walls and ramparts of Jerusalem became sorrowful over their demolition and the ruin of their city.
Sunk: submerged.
Her bars: the wide beams in the gates.

When Babylon attacked, it broke the gates of Jerusalem and burned them, so they became ashes in the ground and their feet trampled them, and Babylon seized the king and the chiefs of the city, because the people had departed from the law of God; and the prophets became liars who see no visions of God and do not guide the people.
The daughter of Zion: Jerusalem.

He likens Jerusalem to a daughter, that is, a girl, because of her weakness, for the girl is a symbol of bodily weakness. And he says that her elders, that is, the greatest of those in her, sat on the ground in humiliation and lowliness and kept silence, because they had lost the ability to defend her or to give any counsel for escaping the enemies' attack.

And because of the dreadfulness of what had befallen them of divine discipline and humiliation, they put dust upon their heads, which is an ancient Eastern custom expressing intense sorrow, and they wear around their waists rough garments, which are sackcloth, also as an expression of sorrow.
As for the virgins, who represent hope and joy, humiliation covered them and they bowed their heads toward the ground.
Fail: grow very weary.
Troubled: violently disturbed.
My liver is poured upon the earth: my inward parts fell on the ground, an expression that symbolizes the loss of all rest and also symbolizes intense sorrow.
The destruction of the daughter of my people: he likens Jerusalem to a weak daughter who has been ground down by the killing of her sons and the humiliation of all who are in her.
Swoon: loss of consciousness.

Jeremiah, of tender feelings, makes clear his intense sorrow in the turmoil of his heart, his continual weeping and his delicate feelings for ruined Jerusalem and the cries of those in her, especially the sight of the children who lose consciousness from hunger as they draw near to death.
Their soul is poured out: they die.

Jeremiah cannot bear the sight of the children who ask their mothers for food and drink, while the mothers are unable to satisfy their hunger, and they keep asking and crying until they lose consciousness and lean on their mothers' bosoms and then die. They fall from hunger in a swoon like those wounded in war.
Equal: I find no city as sorrowful as your sorrow that could be a measure by which the extent of your sorrow is measured, for all sorrows are far less than your sorrow.

Before the sorrows of Jerusalem at Babylon's attack upon her, Jeremiah felt that he had lost any ability to warn her, because she had not listened to God's earlier warnings from his mouth, and he cannot caution her because the Babylonian attack has already come upon her; and as for the extent of the ruin she has suffered, he finds no city like her in it, especially since she was the greatest city in the world, for in her was the temple of the Lord. Consequently her sorrow has no measure because of its intensity, and he feels that her ruin is so wide that it has no limits, like the wide sea, so he finds no word with which to comfort her, but is drowned in his sorrow for her sake. It may be that he means that the Babylonian attack is as strong as the raging sea that drowns everything it meets.
Causes of banishment: false, misleading information that takes the soul away from God.

The prophet makes clear that a basic reason for this ruin is the teaching of the false prophets who spread throughout Jerusalem, so they led the people astray from God and left them to sink into the worship of idols and evil lusts, and gave them a sense of security, so they did not warn them of God's discipline that they might repent. So they remained captives by sin, and they deserved captivity and slavery to Babylon.

Do not flatter people with words that take them away from God, but proclaim the truth in the proper way even if some become angry, and take care to encourage them and bear with them even if they wrong you, so that you win their souls for Christ. Do not seek your own comfort but their salvation, and you will gladden the heart of God, who died for your salvation.
[4] Mockery of her (vv. 15-19)

15- All that pass by clap their hands at thee; they hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, Is this the city that men call The perfection of beauty, The joy of the whole earth? 16- All thine enemies have opened their mouth against thee: they hiss and gnash the teeth: they say, We have swallowed her up: certainly this is the day that we looked for; we have found, we have seen it. 17- The LORD hath done that which he had devised; he hath fulfilled his word that he had commanded in the days of old: he hath thrown down, and hath not pitied: and he hath caused thine enemy to rejoice over thee, he hath set up the horn of thine adversaries. 18- Their heart cried unto the Lord, O wall of the daughter of Zion, let tears run down like a river day and night: give thyself no rest; let not the apple of thine eye cease. 19- Arise, cry out in the night: in the beginning of the watches pour out thine heart like water before the face of the Lord: lift up thy hands toward him for the life of thy young children, that faint for hunger in the top of every street.
Wag: shake, which means mockery.

He makes clear the wretchedness to which Jerusalem came after her destruction, to the point that everyone who passes by her mocks her. He sets out a number of expressions of mockery, such as clapping hands and hissing, proclaiming the dreadfulness of her condition, and wagging heads in contempt for her. And they ask how people used to praise her, saying that her beauty was perfect and that she was a joy among all the cities, for her appearance became utterly vile after her ruin.
Gnash the teeth: they grind their teeth as a sign of mockery and gloating.

From another side, he shows the mockery and gloating of the enemies, harsh upon Jerusalem. They express this by opening their mouths, that is, intense astonishment and contempt, and they hiss and gnash their teeth and rejoice that they have destroyed Jerusalem and that they had longed for this for a long time, that is, the subjection of the whole world to Babylon. So too the neighbors who are jealous of the greatness of Jerusalem gloat over her.
Set up: raised.

Jeremiah affirms that all this destruction is the fulfillment of God's purposes as discipline for His people. He promised from the days of the fathers and of Moses the prophet a reward for the one who obeys His commandments and punishment for the one who breaks them, as He proclaimed the blessings and the curses at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal (Deut 27:12, 13). So God disciplined His people severely that they might repent, and the strength of the enemies who struck Jerusalem appeared, which is symbolized by the horn, because it is the strongest thing in an animal.

Before the mockery and gloating of all against Jerusalem, she finds before her none but God to cry out to, that He may forgive her and remove the punishment from her, and in her remorse she weeps much, so much that he likened the abundance of her tears to a flowing river. He proclaims this sorrow through the ruined wall of Jerusalem, which weeps much; that is, Jerusalem says to God that she has lost all her protection and has no helper but God. And the prophet encourages her to continue weeping and remorse that she may obtain the mercies of God.
Watch: a part of the night; the night is divided into three or four watches.

The prophet continues encouraging Jerusalem to remorse, that she may offer repentance not only in the daytime but also at night from its beginning, that is, in the first watch, offering repentance with tears and lifting her hands in supplication, especially when she sees her children losing consciousness from so much hunger and almost dying.

When tribulation comes upon you, I wish you would not murmur or be troubled over what you have lost, but understand God's purposes and offer repentance, remembering your sins, and be remorseful with tears and prostrations, and make promises of a new life with Him, and you will regain your peace and rest.
[5] A cry to God (vv. 20-22)

20- Behold, O LORD, and consider to whom thou hast done this. Shall the women eat their fruit, and children of a span long? shall the priest and the prophet be slain in the sanctuary of the Lord? 21- The young and the old lie on the ground in the streets: my virgins and my young men are fallen by the sword; thou hast slain them in the day of thine anger; thou hast killed, and not pitied. 22- Thou hast called as in a solemn day my terrors round about, so that in the day of the LORD's anger none escaped nor remained: those that I have swaddled and brought up hath mine enemy consumed.
Children of a span long: that is, sucklings.

Jerusalem cries out from the intensity of the pain and reminds God that she is His daughter, so why did He humiliate her to this degree? She of course knows that this is divine discipline so that she may repent, but she cannot easily accept this humiliation to which she has come, for from intense hunger the mothers ate their infant children. And the Babylonian violence reached the killing of the elders of the people and its prophets who stood for worship in the temple of God.

Jerusalem continues her cry to God, suffering for her young men and her elders, who lie slain and wounded in her streets because of God's severe discipline of her in the day of wrath, that is, by the Babylonian attack upon her.
Solemn day: feast.

Jerusalem likens the crowd and multitude of the slain and wounded among her sons to their having gathered on a day of feast, one of the feasts of the Lord, but they gathered for sorrow, falling wounded and dead; and those who tried to flee were overtaken by the armies of Babylon, that is, the ruin and killing reached every place and every person. Thus Babylon lost her sons who had been raised and grown up in her, who died by the hand of Babylon, and she was in great fear of her enemies.

If you fear God and keep His commandments and keep away from the sources of sin, you become strong and are not troubled by the threats of people, for your God defends you and protects you. So be in constant communion with Him and you will live in assurance. Contrition, hope and repentance: this chapter holds a great place in the rite of the Church, for it is read on one of her most important days, which is Great Friday. It is read at the beginning of the twelfth hour in remembrance of the burial of Christ after His death on the cross; because this chapter is a symbol of Christ, crushed by sufferings for the sake of us sinners. Its words, though they apply to the people of God, Jeremiah writes for the man who speaks; he is crushed and suffers for the sake of his people, a symbol of Christ who suffered and redeemed His people who believe in Him.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Rod: a staff.

Jeremiah feels the sufferings of his people and is crushed with them and for them, though he did not commit their sins; but as a faithful servant with a spirit of fatherhood he feels their sufferings as though they were in him. So the ruin of Jerusalem and her humiliation have come upon him, and he feels that God is the one who disciplines him and his people because of sin, using His rod, which is Babylon, to declare His severe wrath upon His people who persist in sin.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: When Jerusalem was struck, she lost her dwellings and her lamps, and the dust of destruction rose and made the air dark and gloomy. All this was because of their sins, which are symbolized by darkness, for they began to walk in the darkness of sin and lost the lights of their city. All this is an expression of their loss of light, that is, of their not seeing God; so if the people began to walk in sin, God completed their walking in darkness, that is, He disciplined them by the ruin Babylon brought upon them.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: The disciplining hand of God is Babylon, which did not strike them for a time but for many periods, and by all the day he means a long period, months and years, and this is because of the hardness of the heart of the people of God, for they do not return to God by repentance except through many severe disciplines.

Understand God's purposes when a tribulation comes to you, and examine yourself and repent of your sins, to protect yourself from other tribulations to come, and so that you may return to His embrace and enjoy His fatherhood and love. He disciplines you because He loves you, so He does not leave you to perish because of your sins, but disciplines you with gentleness and with severity. So do not murmur but thank Him for His love and return to Him.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah feels, as a representative of his people, that the enemy's blows were many, so that his flesh was filled with bruises and many wounds and his appearance became worn out, and the breaking of his bones means entering into his depths and wronging his inner feelings, because the bones are hidden by the flesh. He is a symbol of Christ hanging on the cross, His blood flowing and the marks of the scourging on His back, and everyone wronged Him, even His loved ones, when they left Him and His disciple betrayed Him. What is meant is not the breaking of bones in the literal sense, for not a bone of Christ was broken, but the meaning is figurative, since these events happened to Jerusalem and Jeremiah attributes them to himself because of his feelings of fatherhood toward them and his sense of them.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Gall: a plant of extreme bitterness. Travail: that is, misery and severe pain. He depicts Babylon's siege of Jerusalem, and the ramparts and towers they built against her and around her, in bitterness and misery, for they deprived the inhabitants of Jerusalem until they were almost dying.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: He likens the darkness in which ruined Jerusalem found herself to the darkness of the grave, since the corpses of her sons were scattered in the streets and the wounded were in the remains of the demolished houses, and this is the natural result of sin, namely death and the darkness of the grave.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Hedged: set up a wall.
Babylon besieged Jerusalem and prevented her people from going out until they were almost dying of hunger, and she became by this like a prisoner bound with chains who cannot move.
So too whoever is lax with sin loses his freedom, and it gains control over him and humiliates him.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah felt the distress of his people, who cried out to God at the Babylonian attack upon them, but God refused his prayer. This is because the prayer was not a prayer of true repentance, but merely distress at Babylon's attack, which caused great distress to the people of God, and this is the discipline God desired that they might turn back from their sins. V. 9: Hewn stones: stones prepared for building with no gaps among them or an outlet for escape. Turned: blocked. It explains what Babylon did with Jerusalem when it built ramparts of hewn stone around her walls, so that if the people fled from the city from intense hunger, the ramparts besieged them and blocked their way, and the armies of Babylon seized them.
Sin hinders a person and blocks his way from righteousness and life with God.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: It is known of the bear that it hides quietly to spring upon its prey, and so does the lion. Here Babylon is likened to the bear and the lion besieging Jerusalem to spring upon her and destroy her. Rather, he sees that it is God who attacks him as discipline for him.
Take care not to make God an enemy to you, and return to Him by repentance and obey His commandments.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Turned aside my ways: made them crooked, so that they lead astray whoever walks in them.

Because of the multitude of the sins of the people of God, God permitted the ways of His people to be crooked, leading to their destruction and the ruin of their cities. For their king Zedekiah allied himself with Egypt and at the same time played the hypocrite to the king of Babylon and pretended to submit to him, so the king of Babylon was angered by his hypocrisy and attacked him and crushed him.

When a person rebels against God, He abandons him and gives him over to a reprobate mind, so he walks in crooked ways that destroy him. So if you have sinned, return to God and do not persist in your snare.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: It shows how cruel the Babylonian attack on Jerusalem was, like one who binds a man and stands him before him, then aims his arrows at him to pierce his body and destroy him.
God will either make you a target for His arrows or a target for His blessings and good things, according to whether you follow Him by keeping His commandments or defy Him by committing sin.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Arrows: darts.
His quiver: a leather case in which the arrows are kept.

He depicts the depth of the wounds that Babylon inflicted on the people of God with arrows that pierced His people to the depths, to rid it of every hidden evil within it. The kidneys are necessary for life, so God wants them to lose their former evil life so that they may live with Him anew in purity.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: All my people: he means all the peoples of the region surrounding the children of Israel.
Because of the ruin of Jerusalem, her neighbors gloated over her and mocked her. By all the day he means the continuation of the mockery.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Bitternesses: plural of bitter, meaning many tribulations.
Wormwood: a bitter and poisonous plant.

The destruction that came upon Jerusalem is a great tribulation, which he likens to a person who ate so much that he was full, that is, Jerusalem was filled with tribulation, and poisons even spread through her body, so many of her sons died.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Broken: smashed. Covered me: Jeremiah likens Jerusalem to a man whom God forced to eat gravel, so his teeth were broken. And He did not only put gravel in his mouth, but filled it and covered it with ashes, because Babylon burned Jerusalem and her streets were filled with ashes, which closed over her inhabitants, who died or fell in a swoon.

A person suffers the consequences of his sins. What he thinks is sweet in sin, he is surprised to find is like gravel that breaks his teeth, and what he thinks is joyful he finds to be ashes, after a person's energies have been burned up by evil, so nothing remains for him but ashes, regret and remorse.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: From the severe distress of Jerusalem, Jeremiah feels that she has lost peace and all her former good things and has fallen into humiliation and contempt.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Despair began to creep into the heart of ruined Jerusalem before His severe discipline.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: And whenever Jerusalem thought of the humiliation to which she had come and her straying from God, she felt a great bitterness like the bitterness of the plants of wormwood and gall.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: And by these painful remembrances the soul of Jeremiah, or of Jerusalem, is bowed down, that is, it is broken, humbled and crushed.
[2] His hope in the Lord (21-38)

21- This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. 22- It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. 23- They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness. 24- The LORD is my portion, saith my soul; therefore will I hope in him. 25- The LORD is good unto them that wait for him, to the soul that seeketh him. 26- It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD. 27- It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth. 28- He sitteth alone and keepeth silence, because he hath borne it upon him. 29- He putteth his mouth in the dust; if so be there may be hope. 30- He giveth his cheek to him that smiteth him: he is filled full with reproach. 31- For the Lord will not cast off for ever: 32- But though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies. 33- For he doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men. 34- To crush under his feet all the prisoners of the earth, 35- To turn aside the right of a man before the face of the most High, 36- To subvert a man in his cause, the Lord approveth not. 37- Who is he that saith, and it cometh to pass, when the Lord commandeth it not? 38- Out of the mouth of the most High proceedeth not evil and good?

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: This: the sufferings by which the soul of Jeremiah was distressed for the sake of his people.

When Jeremiah recalls the sufferings through which his people are passing, he does not despair or murmur, because he hopes in God, believing that He will remove these tribulations from his people, and will comfort and support His prophet Jeremiah, and will bring his people back from captivity and glorify him.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: With the simple eye Jeremiah sees the grace that he enjoys, which is that, although many of the people of God died and the rest were greatly distressed, the whole people was not consumed. The sins of the people deserve the death of all, but God's mercies preserved a remnant for His people so that they might repent, and He would bless them and compensate them for all that was past.

I wish you would thank God for the blessings you enjoy however much tribulations surround you, for by this you show your sonship to God and your clinging to Him by bearing sufferings, and as you thank Him you enjoy His care and His abundant blessings.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: He declares that God's mercies and gifts are renewed for man every day: He makes His sun rise and gives His air to all, and establishes the earth and covers it with the heavens, and bridles the sea so that it does not flood the earth. He is the Controller of all and the One who cares for man, so how much He deserves thanks. God is faithful in His love and fatherhood toward man, however much he sins against Him or falls short in his relationship with Him; however much man offends and neglects his sonship to God, God remains in His fatherhood seeking the salvation of all until the end of life.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Because of the instability of the world and material things, the prophet chose the good portion, which is the love of God, and God is his portion, that is, his goal and his aim, so he runs to Him and enjoys fellowship with Him and is not disturbed over any material loss, because God compensates him. And because of man's attachment to God, whatever tribulations come upon him, his hope remains firm in God.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: God's mercies are given to the one who has hope in God and faith in Him, so a person does not see God's mercy and the abundance of His love unless he believes in Him and seeks Him.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Hope requires trust in God's promises, so he waits for His kindnesses however long the tribulations continue, and remains silent however much others reproach him, because God will intervene in the end and glorify His children who are patient and strive in His way.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Yoke: a crosswise piece of wood placed on the necks of the two animals that pull agricultural implements, and it is a symbol of bearing sufferings.

Jeremiah views sufferings as necessary for forming a person's character and giving him spiritual firmness, so he calls to the ardent youth, full of vitality, not to murmur at bearing sufferings but to accept them in his youth, that he may have a strong and successful character with God and men.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: He depicts the strong man's endurance of sufferings by his silence, patiently bearing them and sitting alone, set apart from all comfort, so he receives consolation and blessing in the end.
This verse and the one before it are a clear prophecy about Christ, who carried the cross while a young man, and everyone stood against Him crying out, Crucify Him, while He did not open His mouth.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: When sufferings increase upon a person, he humbles himself to the ground and the dust, which is expressed here by his mouth being filled with dust, and he endures, but despair fights him, so he says, if so be there may be hope, that is, he may be fought by doubting hope, but he remains clinging to God, and He saves him in the end.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Among the hardest sufferings are psychological sufferings such as blows on the face and reproach, but a person's steadfastness in his faith is rewarded in the end by God with many glories, and here the prophecy is clear about the blows, insults and reproaches that Christ bore at His arrest and crucifixion.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah affirms that God does not reject His children forever, but abandons them for a time that they may repent, then returns and has mercy on them and compensates them for their labors. This appeared on the cross, and Christ expressed it by His saying, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" But after His death He rose with great power.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Although God permits the sorrow of His children for a time, He returns and has mercy on them with His many mercies.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: God never intends from His heart to humiliate His children and grieve them, but He suffers for their sufferings, yet permits tribulations until they repent, then rewards them and compensates them.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Injustices may occur on earth, and a person may seize others and put them in captivity and humiliate them, which is expressed by trampling them, but God permits this for a time to discipline His children, then has mercy on them; as for the oppressor, He punishes him severely, that perhaps he may repent.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Among the well-known injustices is that a person steals another's right and accuses him falsely and punishes another who is wronged, as happened with Christ at His crucifixion though He was without sin, but God in the end removes all this, and He is watching all that happens.

Do not be troubled at the multitude of your tribulations, because your God sees everything closely and supports you until you endure, then glorifies you with glories that cannot be expressed on earth or in heaven.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: The oppressor thinks that God does not see him, so he turns the facts upside down and lies in order to take away the rights of others, but God must punish him, because God is just.
If you have authority, do not use it for your own benefit and pervert justice, especially if the one before you is unable to resist you, and fear his God, because He defends him.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: He declares a clear truth in the end, which is that God is the Controller of all, who permits all these tribulations for the good of His children, that they may repent and be rid of their sins and increase in spiritual strength.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: By evils he means that God permits injustice, but of course does not approve of it, and He is the mover of works of good through His pious children, for it is God who permits good and evil and directs everything for the good of His children.
[3] The need for repentance (vv. 39-54)

39- Wherefore doth a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins? 40- Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD. 41- Let us lift up our heart with our hands unto God in the heavens. 42- We have transgressed and have rebelled: thou hast not pardoned. 43- Thou hast covered with anger, and persecuted us: thou hast slain, thou hast not pitied. 44- Thou hast covered thyself with a cloud, that our prayer should not pass through. 45- Thou hast made us as the offscouring and refuse in the midst of the people. 46- All our enemies have opened their mouths against us.

47- Fear and a snare is come upon us, desolation and destruction. 48- Mine eye runneth down with rivers of water for the destruction of the daughter of my people. 49- Mine eye trickleth down, and ceaseth not, without any intermission, 50- Till the LORD look down, and behold from heaven.
51- Mine eye affecteth mine heart because of all the daughters of my city. 52- Mine enemies chased me sore, like a bird, without cause.
53- They have cut off my life in the dungeon, and cast a stone upon me. 54- Waters flowed over mine head; then I said, I am cut off.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Punishment: chastisement. Jeremiah marvels at his people's murmuring over the destruction that Babylon wrought in Jerusalem and Judea, and depicts Jerusalem as a man, a living human being, on whom blows fall, striking some of his members and wounding another; but sadly Jerusalem did not understand that this tribulation is discipline from God for her sins so that she may repent. This trial is a punishment from God for their sins so that she may take heed and return to Him. It was better for Jerusalem to become strong like a man in his strength and stand against her sins and abstain from them, offering true, earnest repentance.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Let us search our ways: calling ourselves to account. The prophet offers the solution, which is calling oneself to account and returning to God, then testing oneself through conduct in repentance, that a person may know the extent of his submission to God and his rejection of sin.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: He completes the signs of repentance, which is that it be joined with prayer, for repentance is not only leaving sin but establishing a relationship of love with God, and he calls on his people not only to lift their hands to God but their hearts also, that is, to leave off outward, superficial worship and worship God in depth.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: He affirms in the end that the reason God does not pardon His people and punishes them is their sins against God.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Covered: you wrapped yourself in a covering, which is the quilt.

When a person covers himself with the quilt, his body does not appear but only the covering, so he borrows the wrath in place of the quilt, and God is covered with it, that is, nothing appears to man except the wrath of God, and this is what happened in the destruction of Jerusalem by the hand of Babylon and the cruel killing of her sons.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Then he declares that God also covered Himself with the cloud, behind which man cannot see, that is, when God covered Himself with the cloud He became distant from man and did not accept his prayer, because there was no repentance in it but merely a request to be rid of distress.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Part of God's discipline is that He made Jerusalem appear in lowliness after her destruction in the midst of all the peoples around her, whom she had been greater than, and now she is lowlier than all because of sin.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Likewise the enemies around us mocked, and among the signs of mockery and astonishment is the opening of the mouth at seeing the destruction of Jerusalem. All this is a symbol of what happened with Christ when He bore our sins and their punishment on the cross without murmuring, and endured reproach and mockery for our redemption, for what should have come upon us He bore for us.

I wish your contemplation of Christ's redemption would produce in you constant thanks to Him and enjoyment of your new life in Him, and your readiness to bear sufferings for the sake of those around you, even if you are falsely accused in place of those around you in order to cover for them.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: He makes clear the feelings of the Jews at the Babylonian attack upon them, which were fear and terror, because Babylon was cruel and killed many.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah found nothing before him but to weep bitterly in sorrow for his stricken people. Although he knew that this was the punishment of their sins, his fatherhood stirred his inward parts to bitter weeping.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: And the prophet continued in his weeping, because the Babylonian destruction went on for years, but this was necessary in order that the people might repent and return to God.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: All this weeping was not despair, that is, sorrow without benefit, but supplication to God to accept the people's repentance and look upon them with an eye of tenderness and forgive them.

And here appears the role of the servant who comes forward as a representative of his people to ask God's mercies for them, considering himself to be the sinner who needs repentance, and by this he is a symbol of Christ, who did no sin and died for our salvation.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: The prophet shows that his tears are not outward and superficial but flow from the heart because of the contrition and humiliation of his people, and he depicts them as daughters, that is, having no bodily strength before the cruelty of Babylon.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Here Jeremiah speaks of himself when sufferings fell upon him and he was taken captive to Babylon without having sinned, but God intervened, so they took heed and brought him back to Jerusalem according to his wish, and he here is a symbol of Christ, who died without sin and returned alive and rose from the dead.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Dungeon: a deep pit.
Cut off: removed and destroyed.
What happened to Jerusalem in her destruction he likens to the burial of a man in the grave, for Babylon wanted to crush the Jews so that they would have no rising again after that.
And this is what the Jews did to Christ, for they were not content with torturing Him but killed Him and put Him in the tomb.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah likens Jerusalem to a man drowning in water until his head is covered, so he perishes, and this is what happened in the destruction of Jerusalem and in the death of Christ. Therefore we Christians die with Christ by burial in the water of Baptism, then rise by His power to a new life and a new nature.
[4] A cry to God (vv. 55-66)

55- I called upon thy name, O LORD, out of the low dungeon. 56- Thou hast heard my voice: hide not thine ear at my breathing, at my cry. 57- Thou drewest near in the day that I called upon thee: thou saidst, Fear not. 58- O Lord, thou hast pleaded the causes of my soul; thou hast redeemed my life. 59- O LORD, thou hast seen my wrong: judge thou my cause. 60- Thou hast seen all their vengeance and all their imaginations against me.
61- Thou hast heard their reproach, O LORD, and all their imaginations against me; 62- The lips of those that rose up against me, and their device against me all the day.
63- Behold their sitting down, and their rising up; I am their musick. 64- Render unto them a recompence, O LORD, according to the work of their hands.
65- Give them sorrow of heart, thy curse unto them. 66- Persecute and destroy them in anger from under the heavens of the LORD.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: The king of Judah threw Jeremiah into the dungeon, and he prayed to God, then they brought him out and delivered him, as a type of Christ who descended into Hades as a representative of us, but by the power of His divinity ascended to Paradise and the Kingdom. It is noticeable that he mentions the low dungeon, and this means there are depths, or degrees, in torment. Just as in heaven there are many mansions and degrees, so also in eternal torment, and this is because, although the punishment of sin is death, not every sin is like another, and consequently its punishment increases according to its heinousness, among the unbelieving and the unrepentant who go to Hades and eternal torment.

God loves you, and if you fall into the hardest tribulations and call upon Him, He answers you and saves you and does the impossible for you. So do not doubt, and seek Him earnestly, because He is your Father.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: My breathing: the air that goes out of the nose, and by it he means its going out with a sound, that is, sighing and groaning, seeking the help of God.

The prophet declares his assurance that God hears his prayer and feels his pains and sufferings, so he continues his prayer, asking God to take heed of all his inner stored-up sufferings, which come out in sighs or appear in crying and supplication to God.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Thou drewest near: thou approached. When God heard the cry of His people or the prayer of His prophet Jeremiah, He drew near and reassured him that he need not fear.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: God stood as an adversary before the enemies of His people and delivered His children from the slavery of Babylon by raising up the empire of the Medes and Persia, which brought His people back to their country, and thus the slavery of the people of God was loosed, as Christ loosed His people from the chains of sin and perdition, opening to them the door of salvation and eternal life.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah calls God to witness the injustices that came upon him and asks Him to plead his cause, that is, to defend him and restore his glory, and this is what happened by the return from captivity and by the resurrection of the Lord of glory Jesus Christ as the firstborn among many brethren, that we also may rise in Him from every sin by repentance, and God removes from us the wars of the devil our adversary and delivers us from his hand.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah continues his words, calling God to witness all the injustices and Babylon's vengeance on Jerusalem and Judea, that God may have compassion and remove this punishment from His children.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: And Jeremiah says to God that He heard Babylon's reproaches and its imaginations of evil against Jerusalem, and he says this to move God's mercies for His poor people, as God heard the reproaches of the wicked and their torture of Christ, so He glorifies His Son and punishes the wicked.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: The chiefs and people of the kingdom of Judah continued their reproach of Jeremiah and their attempt to kill him for many days, which is expressed by all the day, as the Jews did to Christ.
Do not be troubled when the wicked persist in their evil and reproach you. Do not doubt, but stand firm in your faith, for their apparent strength passes away, and God will glorify you in the end.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: He asks God's help and fatherhood to look upon the plots of his enemies against him, whether in their sitting to conspire against him or their standing to take steps against him, and to deliver him from their hands after he has become the object of their mockery and their first concern, how to be rid of him; and by their musick is meant their repeated speaking evil of him and attempting to kill him. This is what happened with Jeremiah, who was a symbol of Christ in His sufferings.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Jeremiah entreats God to take vengeance on evil and punish the enemies, that perhaps they may believe in the power of God who defends His children, and he does not mean rage and vengeance on the enemies but the proclamation of God's power, His right and His authority over evil.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: Blindness of heart: inability to discern.

If a person continues in his stubbornness and disobedience, God abandons him and gives him over to a reprobate mind (Rom: 28). So Jeremiah asks God to punish the enemies by abandoning them so that they lose their discernment, and when the curses come upon them they may feel their weakness, and so believe in God and live with Him.

entries.section: (1) The contrition of the people of God

paragraphs.text: He completes his appeal to God to discipline the enemies, that He keep pursuing their lives with wrath and destruction, to wipe out their evil from under the heavens, to purify the earth and show God alone as God of gods.
The abasement and destruction of Jerusalem
Dim: lost its beauty, strength and splendor.

Most fine gold: pure gold. The prophet marvels at the ruin of the temple of God, built of great stones and overlaid with pure gold, and how the gold fell into the dust and lost its luster, and the stones of the temple walls were scattered in the streets around it. All this is the result of the Babylonian attack that destroyed the temple of Solomon.

The Babylonians did not only tear down the temple of God and break the gold in it, but also crushed the Jews who believed in God, who had great value among the peoples, for their value was like gold and better than it. These Jews were slain and fell wounded because of their departing from God and neglecting Him.
Jackals: an animal that lives in abandoned places, its size between that of the fox and the wolf.
Breasts: plural of breast, with which the female nurses her child.
Her young ones: her children.

Cruel: harsh. When the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem she became a ruin and was filled with wild and savage animals such as jackals, which take care to nurse their young; but Jerusalem, because of the Babylonian siege upon her, found no food with which to feed her children, so she left them to die, as the ostrich flees and leaves its eggs that it laid and prepared for in the dust, covering them with it, when it senses danger and flees from the hunters. That is, he represents Jerusalem as a mother who became harsh to her children and left them to die of hunger or by the sword of Babylon.

The prophet shows the cruelty of the hunger to which Jerusalem was exposed during Babylon's siege of her, and how the mouths of the infants dried up for lack of water. And the children ask their parents to give them bread, and the fathers find no bread to break and give small pieces of it to their children so that they may not die.

Scarlet: a dark red color, and what is meant is the scarlet garments worn by the great and the rich. He continues his description of the cruelty of the famine in Jerusalem, and the prophet says that the rich of Jerusalem, who used to eat sumptuous foods, found no bread or water in the time of hunger. They used to wear luxurious garments of scarlet, purple and other clothing of the wealthy, but now they have fallen in the streets in the dust, groaning and dying of hunger and thirst.

Punishment: chastisement. The prophet remembers the ruin of Sodom, which burned because of its evil, and says that the state of Jerusalem is harder than that of Sodom, for the enemy attacked her after besieging her and killed and wounded those in her, whereas the people of Sodom died without the hand of enemies; but in the case of Jerusalem, God used the hand of Babylon to discipline them severely, that perhaps they might repent.

Do not hate the one who troubles you, and do not murmur at trials, but accept them from the hand of God and remember your sins, for perhaps they are the cause, so you return to Him by repentance, and then He removes all your troubles from you and even rewards you with many blessings for your repentance and your supplication to Him.
Her Nazarites: persons who vow themselves to God for a certain period which they spend in fasting and prayer, so God gives them splendor and grace.
Rubies: a kind of precious stone, its color tending to red, found in the seas such as the Red Sea.
Their polishing: their bodies.

Like sapphire: a kind of precious stone, transparent, tending to blue and distinguished by hardness. He describes those who worship God in His holy temple in Jerusalem, who present themselves as Nazarites to God, and who were distinguished by purity like pure snow, and God gives them grace so their faces become white as milk, and they were full of vitality, and their bodies tended to redness like the stones of coral and like the sapphire, beautiful in appearance and tending to a light blue. That is, the Jews who believed in God enjoyed purity, vitality and whiteness, and the color red, which symbolizes love and self-giving, and the color blue, which symbolizes heaven. These who worshiped God perished by the hand of Babylon because they neglected their worship and were occupied with the worship of idols.

When Babylon attacked Jerusalem and destroyed the city, and its inhabitants fell wounded and slain by hunger and by the sword, their appearance became black like the darkness, and when they fell in the streets it was no longer easy to recognize them, because their appearance changed through hunger, for their bodies became very thin and their skin clung to their bones, and their flesh had vanished from weakness, and their appearance became like a dry piece of wood.

V. 9: The Jews who died by the sword of Babylon were in a better state than the Jews who were tormented by hunger, for they found no fruits of the field to eat because of the siege of Jerusalem, and in the end they died a very painful death.

The pitiful: plural of tender one, for the mother is distinguished by tenderness toward her children by the instinct of motherhood. Among the most horrible scenes that occurred in the famine in Jerusalem at Babylon's siege of her was that from intense hunger the mothers cooked their infant children and ate them.
Zion: an ancient name for Jerusalem. Thus God took care to discipline Jerusalem, and when His wrath came upon her, Babylon destroyed her and burned her temple and her palaces.

Because of the greatness of Jerusalem and the strength of her temple and the presence of God in it, the peoples around her were astonished at the attack of the Babylonian enemy upon her and her destruction.
[2] The destruction of Jerusalem because of her sins (vv. 13-20)

13- For the sins of her prophets, and the iniquities of her priests, that have shed the blood of the just in the midst of her, 14- They have wandered as blind men in the streets, they have polluted themselves with blood, so that men could not touch their garments. 15- They cried unto them, Depart ye; it is unclean; depart, depart, touch not: when they fled away and wandered, they said among the heathen, They shall no more sojourn there. 16- The anger of the LORD hath divided them; he will no more regard them: they respected not the persons of the priests, they favoured not the elders. 17- As for us, our eyes as yet failed for our vain help: in our watching we have watched for a nation that could not save us. 18- They hunt our steps, that we cannot go in our streets: our end is near, our days are fulfilled; for our end is come. 19- Our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of the heaven: they pursued us upon the mountains, they laid wait for us in the wilderness. 20- The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the LORD, was taken in their pits, of whom we said, Under his shadow we shall live among the heathen.

The prophet makes clear the reason for the destruction of Jerusalem, which is the sins of her false prophets who led the people astray, and also the priests who condemned the innocent to death, such as their attempt to kill Jeremiah

He declares that the leaders of the Jewish people no longer see the truth, that is, God, that is, they became blind to the knowledge of God, and evil covered them, that is, they became guilty against God, and the blood of those whom they killed cries out before God, so they became more unclean than the lepers who go outside the cities and cry, Unclean, unclean, so that no one comes near them and touches them and becomes unclean.

He likens the leaders of the Jews at their flight from Jerusalem to the unclean lepers who live outside the inhabited cities, so that every person keeps away from them. In the same way the nations kept away from the fleeing Jews, lest the sword of Babylon strike them, and the nations felt that Jerusalem would not be inhabited afterward, because her ruin was great.

Hath divided them: scattered them. He makes clear that the Jews' flight was from God, who permitted Babylon to attack them, so they are scattered over the earth, whether by fleeing or by being taken captive by the Babylonians, and all this was because of their sins, for they did not honor the priests or the elders, but speech became for selfishness, evil and cruelty.
Failed: grew weary.

Jeremiah expresses the state of his people, who had allied with Egypt. When Babylon besieged Jerusalem, the Jews waited for help to come to them from Egypt but found none, and when the Jews hid in their towers and fortresses from the face of Babylon, they waited for Egypt to save them, but it did not come to them, to show the vanity of relying on men. It would have been better for them to trust in God alone, since the idol gods they worshiped did not help them.

Do not let your eyes be deceived by money or position or all the powers of the world, for they are worthless when God permits your discipline. Return to Him by repentance and you will obtain His mercies, and I wish you would not leave Him again, so that you are not exposed to these disciplines, and thank Him for His discipline because He loves you and seeks the salvation of your soul; if you do not understand from His gifts, He permits discipline.

Babylon attacked Jerusalem, so the Jews fled and hid in every corner, because the armies of Babylon set snares everywhere to seize the Jews and kill them. Thus the Jews lost their freedom of movement in their ways and the squares of the city.
Laid wait: hid. Pursued: hastened after them.

The Babylonian soldiers pursued the Jews everywhere, and when the Jews tried to flee, they hastened after them and overtook them, because they were extremely swift like the eagles, and even when the Jews went to hide in the mountains the Babylonians pursued them there, and in the wilderness the Babylonians hid to pounce on the Jews and seize them if they passed through the wilderness.
The breath of our nostrils: the most important person we have, who gives us life, because breathing is an essential process for life; the anointed of the Lord is likened to it.
Their pits: their snares with which they hunt us.

This is a clear prophecy about Christ when the Jews seized Him and delivered Him to be crucified. He was the hope of the people for delivering them from the Romans, and they found the Romans crucifying Him, and the Jews did not understand that He came to redeem them from sin and to die for them. This verse also applies to the king of Judah, Zedekiah, whom Babylon seized and killed his sons before his eyes, then put out his eyes, and it applies also to all the chiefs of Judah and their prophets, and it applies also to Jeremiah, for Babylon seized all of them and killed some of them.
[3] The discipline of gloating Edom (vv. 21, 22)
21- Rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Edom, that dwellest in the land of Uz; the cup also shall pass through unto thee: thou shalt be drunken, and shalt make thyself naked.
22- The punishment of thine iniquity is accomplished, O daughter of Zion; he will no more carry thee away into captivity: he will visit thine iniquity, O daughter of Edom; he will discover thy sins.

God mocks the offspring of Edom, that is, the offspring of Esau, who dwell next to the children of Israel, south of the land of the Jews in the region of the mountains of Seir. He says to the land of Edom, mocking it, let it go on in its joy and merriment since it gloated over the fall of Jerusalem, and warns it that He will discipline it and it also will fall by the hand of Babylon, because it gloated over the calamity of its brothers the Jews.

If you see your brother meeting a problem and distress, pray for him and do not reproach him or gloat over him, for if you humble yourself before God, He will keep you and save you from distresses; and if your heart is filled with evil toward your brothers, know that God is just and will repay you for your evil.

God reassures His people when He calls her daughter of Zion, declaring that her discipline by captivity for her iniquities is accomplished and she will not be disciplined by other distresses; on the contrary, after a time the captivity will end and she will return to her land honored, and on the contrary, Edom, which gloated over her, will be punished for her sins and for her gloating. God saves His humiliated children
Behold: look out from the balcony.
The last chapter is a prayer more than a lament, in which he entreats God to look upon the bad state of His people and the shame into which they have come.

The first thing God notices, or Jeremiah asks of Him, is that He deliver them from the Babylonian occupation that seized their houses and fields and all that they own, and this is what Satan does with the one who is lax toward sin, for he robs him of his abilities.

After the men of the kingdom of Judah were killed, the children became orphans and their mothers widows, that is, they became weak, without strength, for the person who has fallen into sin has lost the power of God working in him, because he rejected God, so God abandoned him.

The Babylonian enemy pressed upon Jerusalem, besieged, or after she fell into their hands and they killed her men, so the necessities of life such as water were not available, and they bought it, because of its scarcity, at a high price which is expressed by silver, and even wood, that is, sticks of dry plants used for lighting fire, which is considered very cheap and without price; that is, the cost was extreme and the necessities of man were unavailable. This is what Satan does to keep us away from God, the source of our life, for the Holy Spirit is the spring of our water and the fire that burns our sins.

The Babylonians enslaved the people of God and put the yoke on their necks to work as forced labor, or beat them with staves on their necks and drove them out of their cities, and despite the work and much toil they did not obtain the necessary sustenance.

In the distress of hunger in which the Jews found themselves, they tried to ask help from Egypt or Assyria to obtain bread, that is, the necessities of life, but no one came to their aid, and it would have been better for them to take refuge in God and not trust in the arm of flesh. When they repented and returned to God, He brought them back from captivity.
